entries.english:
Appeal before the Imperial Chamber Court concerning the reversion of male fiefs. Plaintiff/applicant/intervenor: Graf Heinrich zu Castell; Graf Konrad zu Castell was defendant in the first instance. Defendants/intervenors and agnatic fief heirs of Gabriel von Heßberg zu Weitersroda are Hektor von Heßberg zu Brunn; Christoph zu Eishausen; Hans Wilhelm zu Bedheim; Friedrich Albrecht zu Schnodsenbach; Klaus zu Weimarschmieden; Hans Andreas and Hans Albrecht zu Reurieth; and Christoph Philipp, Klaus, Beringer, Friedrich, and Ernst zu Eishausen, sons of Hans von Heßberg zu Eishausen. Hektor acted under powers of attorney from Christoph, Hans Wolf, Hans Wilhelm, Friedrich Albrecht, Klaus, Hans, Hans Andreas, and Hans Albrecht von Heßberg, plaintiffs in the first instance. Plaintiff’s counsel were Lic. Jakob Streitt (1588), Dr. Sebastian Wolf (1596), Lic. Peter Paul Steurnagel (1603), Dr. Friedrich Plönnies with substitute Dr. Johann Georg von Gülchen (1671), and Dr. Georg Friedrich Müeg with substitute Dr. Johann Friedrich Stieber (1686). Defendants’ counsel were Dr. Johann Jakob Kremer (1577), Dr. Lukas Goll (1630), and Dr. Henrich Wilhelm Erhardt with substitute Dr. Johann Hermann Schaffer (1672).

The case was an appeal concerning the reversion of male fiefs. In the first instance, after Gabriel von Heßberg died as Bernhard von Heßberg’s last male descendant, Graf Konrad zu Castell declared Gabriel’s fiefs at Rödelsee, Prühl (called Brüel in the file), and Fröhstockheim reverted. In mid-November 1575 the agnates and fief heirs applied to the fief court established by the Counts of Castell at Wiesenbronn for enfeoffment. They argued that because Castell held its fiefs from the Bishopric of Würzburg, the count’s house had to observe the local fief custom in its dealings with its own vassals: a fief remained in a lineage until the lineage was completely extinct, whether or not male descendants of the original recipient were still alive. The plaintiff relied on contrary imperial fief custom, also followed in the Margraviate of Brandenburg and the Bishopric of Eichstätt. In the fief proceeding the defendants obtained an imperial commission for the taking of evidence in late August 1579, and the plaintiff’s house obtained another in mid-November 1582. In late September 1590 the count’s house was ordered to enfeoff the defendants with the disputed properties and the revenues that had accrued since the litigation was joined. Both sides maintained their first-instance positions. The proceedings were first heard by the Castell fief court at Wiesenbronn in 1575 and then by the Imperial Chamber Court, 1591–1687.

The earlier file (Q 7/8) includes the 1525 purchase deed and register for properties at Rödelsee, Fröhstockheim, Großlangheim, Prühl, Herpersdorf, Birkach auf der Heide, Mainstockheim, and Nenzenheim, sold by Marx von Berlichingen and his wife Margaretha von Schaumberg to Bernhard von Heßberg and his wife Ottilia von Seckendorf. It also contains evidence gathered in two imperial commissions. The Hesseberg petition led to the 1579–1580 commission assigned to Sebastian Wunderlin, town scribe of Windsheim. Witnesses in 1580 included Konrad von Rosenberg, Georg Ludwig von Seinsheim, Veit Erasmus von Eyb, Christoph Truchseß von Pommersfelden, Joachim von Seckendorf, Hans Joachim Stiebar von Buttenheim, Hans Zobel von Giebelstadt, Valentin and Eyrich von Münster, Heinrich and Hans von Bibra, Hans Nikolaus and Christoph von Schaumberg, Wilhelm, Hans Christoph and Hans von Egloffstein, Georg von Heldritt, Lorenz von Guttenberg, Georg Marschall von Ebneth, Hektor von Rabenstein, and Joachim von Redwitz. The commission obtained by Castell in 1582–1583 was assigned to Johann Adler, a citizen of Schweinfurt. Its witnesses included Michael Strauß and Valentin Boxberger, chancellor and secretary to the Counts of Henneberg; Christoph Tettelbach, Nikolaus Stadtmann, Sebastian Pürckel, Andreas Mußmann, and Kaspar Rauchbar, chancellor, chamberlain, councillor, or secretary to the Margraves of Brandenburg; Tobias Frankmann and Philipp Luchs, chancellor and councillor to the Fürstbischof of Eichstätt; and Sigmund Rößlein, senior bailiff of Limpurg at Gaildorf.

The earlier file also collects records concerning other fiefs: for Rödelsee and Fröhstockheim, a 1573 purchase by Graf Georg Ernst of Henneberg-Schleusingen from Ernst von Crailsheim and its fief acknowledgment; for Aschbach Castle, a 1527 fief charter from Graf Wilhelm of Henneberg-Schleusingen to Albrecht von Vestenberg, acknowledgments by Hans Albrecht von Vestenberg (1537), Hans Wilhelm Fuchs von Bimbach (1559), and Hans Karl Fuchs von Bimbach (1578), and records of the 1543–1559 suit of Anton, later Konrad Christoph von Vestenberg, against Counts Wilhelm, later Georg Ernst and Poppo of Henneberg-Schleusingen. For the Henneberg castle estate there are acknowledgments by Wolf von Wambach (1537) and Matthes von Hönningen (1559). Plankenfels materials include Brandenburg fief-register extracts recording enfeoffments of Ernst von Wichsenstein (1542), Ernst von Rüssenbach (1549), Ulrich von Rüssenbach (1564), and Hans Gilg von Laineck (1573), plus a 1573 fief charter. Göppmannsbühl Castle materials include the 1517 sale from Jobst von Dandorff to Georg von Streitberg and a 1536 sale of the tavern by Hans Ferg genannt Vischer to Friedrich von Streitberg; Brandenburg charters and register extracts concern Kaspar Dandorffer (1488), Adam and Friedrich von Streitberg (1525), Paul, Sigmund, Georg, and Wolf Christoph von Streitberg (1550), Paul and Georg von Streitberg (1561), Paul von Streitberg (1568), Heinrich von Trautenberg (1573), and Hans Rephun, Kastner at Hof (1574), with acknowledgments by Paul von Streitberg (1568) and Rephun (1574). Other records concern half of Gleißenberg Castle (Andreas Mußmann, 1571); Lisberg Castle (Helphant von Giech, 1557, and Hans von Aschhausen, 1577); Vogelsberg, also called Rammersdorf (Hans Zobel von Giebelstadt, 1568); Frankenberg and Michelfeld castles and Nenzenheim village (a 1568 agreement of Markgraf Georg Friedrich of Brandenburg-Ansbach and Brandenburg-Kulmbach with Bernhard von Hutten and Brandenburg fief charters to Bernhard and Georg Ludwig von Hutten); Jochsberg, Triesdorf, Reichenbach, and Bertholdsdorf (the 1572 agreement with Friedrich Joachim von Seckendorf and his fief charters); the Eichstätt fiefs of brothers Heinrich, Wolf, and Hans von Künßberg (Leander von Künßberg’s 1548 acknowledgment); tithes at Kevenhüll, Schweigersdorf, Hainsberg, Oberndorf, Mitteldorf, Mallerstetten, Muttenhofen, and Hebersdorf and the vogt rights at Eismannsdorf (acknowledgments by Hans Joachim, Hans Sigmund, and Hans Georg von Parsberg, 1579); the church patronage at Beyerberg, mass patronage at Königshofen and Wieseth, and tithes (Hans Arnold von Seckendorf, 1558); a pond near Triesdorf (Friedrich Joachim von Seckendorf, 1571); and properties at Königheim (Elisabeth von Hettersdorf’s 1562 request and Hans Braun von der Heydt’s 1573 enfeoffment and acknowledgments).

Attachments to the Heßberg evidentiary brief include fief charters from the Counts of Castell—Johann, Wolfgang, and Konrad—for Bernhard, Raphael, and Gabriel von Heßberg concerning Wiesentheid, Unterlaimbach, Rödelsee, and Prühl (1523–1568); the 1481 agreement of Wiguläus and Eucharius von Heßberg with Hans and Dietz von Heßberg, guardians of Geiso von Heßberg and Katharina von Waldenfels’s children; Castell charters to the defendants for properties and tithes at Rudolzhofen, Burgbernheim, Wiebelsheim, Buchheim, and Bergtshofen (1474–1578); Würzburg bishops Lorenz, Konrad II, Melchior, Friedrich, and Julius’s charters concerning Anfelden tithe, Walldorf Castle, Habichtsburg (called Habsburg in the file), and Breuberg and Ebertshausen (1505–1575); Hohenlohe grants by Eberhard von Hohenlohe-Waldenburg, Ludwig Casimir and Wolfgang von Hohenlohe-Neuenstein concerning Rödelsee Castle and Waltersberg (1568–1577); and Herzog Johann Wilhelm of Saxony-Weimar’s 1571 grant concerning Gleichamberg and Römhild. Further deeds concern the sale of Rudolzhofen tithe by Friedrich Rüdt von Collenberg through Heinrich von Seckendorf and Jakob Zettler of Windsheim to Stephan von Heßberg (1454–1472); Bergtshofen properties sold by Hermann von Messelhausen to Hans von Heßberg and Elisabeth von Seckendorf (1441); Anfelden tithe sold by Sebastian von Lüchau to Karl von Heßberg (1504); and Philipp von Gebsattel’s Würzburg tithe and property grants (1548) and Brandenburg grants at Berolzheim, Vorderpfeinach, and Marktbergel. Consent letters by Bischof Konrad II of Würzburg and Graf Wolfgang zu Castell allow Wolf von Heßberg to assign his wife Kunigunde von Crailsheim’s dowry and counter-dowry to fiefs (1528 and 1530). A 1538 pledge by Wolfgang Freiherr von Schwarzenberg to Georg Friedrich Freiherr von Schwarzenberg concerns half the tithe at Simmershofen, with Graf Wolfgang zu Castell’s consent. Castell’s exceptions include Kurfürst Friedrich I of Brandenburg’s 1431 grant to Erkinger von Seinsheim and Castell fief-register extracts (1384–1506), plus two legal opinions to the fief court, one by Dr. Sebastian Röttinger of Nördlingen (1589).

The Heßberg commission file (Q 25) includes the 1457 agreement with Bischof Johann III of Würzburg making Castell a proper male fief and Graf Wilhelm’s fief acknowledgment; testimony by Hans von Steinau genannt Steinrück and Dietrich von Streitberg (1598); and 1435 and 1461 agreements of Bishops Johann II and Johann III and the cathedral chapter with the Bishopric of Würzburg’s counts and knighthood. Other materials are a 1674 legal opinion from the papers of Nuremberg council legal adviser Dr. Johann Herel, with a certificate from Nuremberg’s mayor and council concerning his origins; 1674 certificates on fief customs from the prince-bishopric courts of Bamberg, Würzburg, and Eichstätt, the Brandenburg courts of Bayreuth and Ansbach, and the Franconian Counts’ College; and the printed *Notitia Actorum in causa Castell contra Heßberg Appellationis* (1676, submitted 12 December). The register records the proceedings as beginning in 1591. Prior courts were the fief courts at Schleusingen and Wiesenbronn; Dr. Johann Herel (d. 1603) provided a legal opinion.
